newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik president to negotiate release of hostages.
newsitem.headline: Tajik president to negotiate release of hostages.

text.p: Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov hoped to hold direct talks on Monday with a rogue group of Islamic rebels still holding six hostages, including U.N. workers.
Presidential spokesman Zafar Saidov said Rakhmonov would go to the village of Obigarm, 80 km (50 miles) east of the capital Dushanbe, to negotiate with brothers Bakhrom and Rizvon Sadirov.

The Sadirovs hold two U.N. military observers -- a Swiss and a Ukrainian -- three workers of the U.N. refugee agency and Tajik Security Minister Saidamir Zukhurov, seized when he tried to negotiate the release of the others.

"Bakhrom said he was ready to negotiate directly with the president and the president readily accepted the proposal," Saidov said, adding that the rebel leader gave assurances the hostages would not be harmed.
"Don't worry about the hostages. Nothing threatens their lives," he quoted Bakhrom Sadirov as saying.
But the two Tajik sides clearly have little trust towards each other and it was only the intervention of Russia which led to negotiations resulting in earlier releases of hostages.
Russia, which views Tajikistan as a barrier against the spread of Islamic fundamentalism, has a considerable military force there and also helps to police its border with Afghanistan.
Moscow backs Rakhmonov, both politically and economically, and has considerable influence over his government.

The crisis erupted on February 4, when Bakhrom Sadirov's rebel group seized hostages and demanded that the government give free passage for his brother Rizvon and some 40 supporters to join him from Afghanistan.
The Tajik authorities allowed more than 30 armed fighters to reach Sadirov's base on Saturday on the understanding that he would then free all his captives.
But the rebels, based at a mountain stronghold about one mile (km) above Obigarm in a remote region of the former Soviet republic, released only three hostages and temporarily broke off negotiations.
They resumed contact on Sunday with mediator Gennady Sizov, a Russian diplomat, and freed another five captives.
Several senior Russians, including Deputy Prime Minsiter Vitaly Ignatenko, have made direct telephone contact with Sadirov but appeared increasingly frustrated with him.
The crisis highlighted the instability of Tajikistan, an impoverished mountainous state bordering Afghanistan and China.
Rakhmonov and the leader of the united Islamist opposition, Sayid Abdullo Nuri, agreed on a ceasefire last December after a four-year civil war in which tens of thousands of people were killed.
The ceasefire seems to be holding, but rogue groups opposed to Rakhmonov are still scattered across the country and some, like those loyal to the Sadirovs, are based in Afghanistan.
Russian media reports said Afghan warlord Ahmad Shah Masood, to whom the Sadirovs were close, had tried to mediate in the hostage crisis and even visited Tajikistan but with no apparent result.
